# The storyboard

The third stop: the script of the whole page, which the person says yes to. Write it to `docs/story/storyboard.md`.

A plan covers what its asker thought to ask for. Most people ask for the idea and for what moves. Nobody asks what the site does on a phone, or without the 3D, or what a shared link shows, and a script that leaves those out is half a script. So this one has a place for each, and an empty place shows.

## The chapters

A row to a chapter:

| Chapter | Its name in the form | The role it holds | What it tells, in a few words | What the pieces do | What you can touch |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

## The beats

Under each chapter, a row to a beat. A beat is one settled state of the scene and one block of text.

| Beat | Screens | How the pieces stand | What is on their faces | What the chapter adds | What its caption stands on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|

- **Screens:** how much scroll the beat takes. One, or more where the scroll works something.
- **How the pieces stand:** a stack, a fan, a ring, a row, a wall, or what the chapter needs. The same pieces in every beat.
- **What is on their faces:** the person's real pictures and words. Name the picture.
- **What the chapter adds:** anything in the scene besides the pieces. Often nothing.
- **What its caption stands on:** a working title of a few words, and the lines of the fact sheet the caption will be written from. Not the caption.

**Write no captions yet.** The words are written at a later stop, where the person chooses them. A sentence written now, to make the script read well, is where a detail gets in that nobody told you: a hall that was "standing empty", a wheel that is "true again". So a beat names its facts and stops there. Where a beat wants something the fact sheet does not hold, such as what the work taught them or what was wrong before they came, put the question in its place.

## Someone with thirty seconds

Say how a visitor who does not scroll gets the name, what the person does, one proof of it, and how to reach them. The first screen carries the first three. A rail jumps to any chapter, and one link skips to the close.

## Without the scene

Say what a visitor gets in each case. The text is ordinary HTML over the scene, so all of it is there in every row. Say what stands in for the pieces.

| Where | What the visitor gets |
|---|---|
| On a phone | |
| With reduced motion | |
| With no WebGL | |
| With no JavaScript | |

## The look and the type

Both come from the object's material: plates are ceramic on linen, a status page is dark glass, a paper is white with dark ink. Name two or three looks, each as its ground, its ink, one accent, and the surface of the pieces. The person picks by scrolling, once it is built.

Two typefaces: one for the text, and one for what is printed on the pieces, which belongs to the form.

## Everything else the site needs

Mark every row build, later or never, and say who decided.

| | Build, later or never | Who decided |
|---|---|---|
| The way round the page | | |
| A page for each project | | |
| Every project listed | | |
| How to reach them, and a CV | | |
| What others say | | |
| Languages | | |
| What a shared link shows, and the site's icon | | |
| The page for an address that is not there | | |
| A blog | | |
| A chat | | |
| A legal notice, where their country asks for one | | |

## What you ask for

A yes to the script, or what to change. Give the list of what you decided for them with it.

item.text:
**Before the menu** will be one continuous story carried by a 3D ferment register. Its question is: **What happens before the menu is written?**

Seven leaves stay present throughout the scroll. They open, separate into informative arrangements and finally bind together again. The movement explains your work: dates become a sequence, log fields become a process, and results become readable evidence.

The complete plan is saved in [storyboard.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-terse-with-XpX4fT/docs/story/storyboard.md). Nothing has been built.

### The whole scroll

| Chapter | What visitors learn | What moves |
|---|---|---|
| **Entry** | Your name, Head Chef at Saltmarsh, fermentation focus and the central question | The register opens, revealing the log fields you use |
| **Started** | Your career, with September 2022 as the Head Chef start and Norway clearly described as an unpaid stage | Leaves spread into a chronological line; the stage leaf comes forward |
| **Salt** | How the prep list and ferment log guide the kitchen | Leaves form a diagram of start date, salt, checks and readiness, then place the menu last |
| **Checks** | The larder, apprentice programme and monthly workshops | Leaves fan into three work panels, using approved photographs where available |
| **Ready** | The whole-kitchen waste result, with its measurement context | Two equal-size leaves show 14 and 5 kg/week; surrounding leaves explain the scope |
| **Notes** | Brine and Callum’s recommendation | Leaves become a reading spread, then reveal the credited quote |
| **Next entry** | The answer: preparation and checking precede the weekly menu | All seven leaves reassemble, beside apprenticeship, workshop and writer enquiry routes |

The desktop scroll would take roughly **ten screen lengths**. Each movement ends in a settled, readable state. On phones, content determines the length.

The opening immediately gives visitors your name, role, evidence of your method and enquiry links. A chapter rail lets them jump anywhere, including straight to contact.

### Visual direction

I recommend **warm paper, charcoal ink and dark olive accents**: a working register with subtle paper texture, fine rules and generous margins.

Use **Source Sans 3** for readable text and **IBM Plex Mono** for dates, quantities and log fields. Two alternative looks are documented: mineral grey with blue accents, or cream with rust accents.

The register is an editorial interpretation of your log. It won’t pretend to reproduce real batch entries, recipes or handwriting.

### Motion and accessibility

Scroll controls the same seven leaves throughout. The camera stays steady while visitors read; there is no forced scrolling or continuous spinning.

All information also exists as ordinary page text:

- **Phone:** a single column with a smaller scene.
- **Reduced motion:** static arrangements without rotation or parallax.
- **No WebGL:** a static register illustration and readable chapter panels.
- **No JavaScript:** the complete page, navigation and contact links still work.

### Content and contact

The waste result uses **“we”**, identifies prep and plate waste, states the one-month measurement in 2023 and explains that bones were excluded.

Priya’s photographs remain pending restaurant permission and require her credit. Olu’s artwork remains pending his permission. Your owned photographs can support the plan after checking labels and any staff faces. Supplier prices stay excluded.

The close offers three routes: apprenticeship enquiries, workshop booking or enquiries, and food-writer contact. Actual addresses and booking destinations are still needed. No CV is planned, given your audience and the fact that you are not job-seeking.

### Scope and later implementation

A future build would use a pre-rendered page with a progressively loaded Three.js scene. It would include chapter navigation, share previews, a log-inspired icon and a missing-page screen. Separate project pages and a blog would wait; chat and tracking are outside the initial scope.

Final public captions are deliberately still unwritten. The storyboard identifies the facts each caption must use so wording can be reviewed without introducing unsupported claims.

I chose the seven-leaf structure, scroll length, recommended visual direction, fonts and fallback approach; those decisions are recorded in [decided-for-you.md](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-terse-with-XpX4fT/docs/story/decided-for-you.md).

**Does this storyboard have your yes, or what would you change?** The [storyfolio skill](/tmp/storyfolio-evals/codex-chef-terse-with-XpX4fT/.agents/skills/storyfolio/SKILL.md) requires your approval of “the script of the whole page” to complete planning. That approval would complete the plan; building would remain a separate request.
